title: Film Toolkit: core study areas, contexts and exam skills

topics.title: Core area 1: key elements of film form

items.definition: Shot scale from extreme long shot to extreme close-up controls how much we see and how close we feel.
items.examples: ELS of the ruins in Pan’s Labyrinth; ECU of Bonnie’s lips; CU of Arthur forcing a smile.
keyFacts: ELS/LS establish place and can make characters look small
MS shows body language and relationships
CU/ECU give psychological insight and intensify emotion
items.examTip: Write the scale AND the effect: “a close-up isolates Arthur’s pain”.

items.definition: High, low, canted (Dutch) and point-of-view angles shape power, stability and alignment.
items.examples: Canted close-up of the dying Ofelia; POV of the Sunken Place; low angle on Renton in the carpet.
keyFacts: Low angle = power or threat; high angle = vulnerability
Canted angle = a world off balance
POV shots align the spectator with a character
items.examTip: Angles are easy marks when tied to meaning.

items.definition: Pans, tilts, tracking, crane, handheld and Steadicam movement create energy, intimacy or control.
items.examples: Handheld chaos in City of God; Curtiz’s crane into the market; Shaun’s long tracking walks.
keyFacts: Handheld = immediacy, instability, documentary feel
Steadicam = smooth, floating, controlled
The spec contrasts handheld with Steadicam technology
items.examTip: Pair movement with editing to describe a sequence’s rhythm.

items.definition: Deep focus keeps foreground and background sharp; shallow focus isolates one plane; focus pulls shift attention.
items.examples: Shallow focus on the victims’ shoes in the Pale Man’s lair; deep focus in City of God’s apartment.
keyFacts: Deep focus lets the spectator choose where to look (Bazin)
Shallow focus directs attention and isolates characters
A rack focus changes meaning within a single shot
items.examTip: Depth of field overlaps with mise-en-scène: the spec says so.

items.definition: Balanced or unbalanced arrangement of the frame, frames within frames and off-screen space create meaning.
items.examples: Bonnie behind the bed-rail “bars”; Chris framed through doorways at the Armitage house.
keyFacts: Rule of thirds and symmetry signal order or control
Unbalanced frames create unease
Frames within frames suggest entrapment
items.examTip: Mention the spec phrase “balanced and unbalanced shots”.

items.definition: Key, fill and backlight model a subject; low-key lighting (little fill) creates shadow and mood.
items.examples: Edeson’s low-key café in Casablanca; low-key subway in Joker; Pan’s Labyrinth’s bottle murder.
keyFacts: High-key = bright, even, optimistic
Chiaroscuro = strong light/dark contrast, from painting
Lighting gives psychological insight into character
items.examTip: “Chiaroscuro” and “three-point lighting” are named in the spec.

items.definition: Palette, filters and colour grading create mood, mark time or separate worlds.
items.examples: Pan’s Labyrinth: cold blue reality vs warm amber fantasy; City of God: warm past, cold present.
keyFacts: Monochrome cinematography is also a spec point
Digital grading allows precise control in post-production
Colour motifs build meaning through repetition
items.examTip: Colour is often the easiest way into aesthetics questions.

items.definition: Locations and objects place the story and carry symbolic meaning, often as repeated motifs.
items.examples: Vidal’s watch; Casablanca’s letters of transit; Get Out’s teacup.
keyFacts: Settings can be naturalistic or expressive
Props can become motifs through patterned repetition
Location shooting vs studio sets is also a context point
items.examTip: Pick a prop and track how its meaning develops.

items.definition: What characters wear and how they look shows identity, status, change and genre.
items.examples: Joker’s red suit; Bonnie’s beret; Vidal’s crisp uniform; the Pale Man’s practical make-up.
keyFacts: Costume change = character change
Make-up can be realistic or expressive (prosthetics)
Costume can define a whole era’s style
items.examTip: Link costume to representation (gender, class).

items.definition: Where actors stand and move (blocking) and what is kept off-screen shape power and suspense.
items.examples: Arthur dancing down the stairs; the rebels hidden in the woods around the mill.
keyFacts: Directing as “choreography” of movement (spec)
Off-screen space builds fear: what we cannot see
Distance between characters shows relationships
items.examTip: Staging is often missed by students: an easy way to stand out.

items.definition: Naturalistic mise-en-scène imitates reality; expressive mise-en-scène exaggerates it to show emotion or ideas.
items.examples: City of God’s real favela vs Pan’s Labyrinth’s fantasy creatures.
keyFacts: Social realism favours naturalism
Expressionism and fantasy favour stylisation
Many films mix both, as Trainspotting does
items.examTip: Useful for aesthetics and realism questions.

items.definition: Invisible editing that keeps space and time clear: shot/reverse shot, eyeline match, match on action, 180° rule.
items.examples: Rick and Ilsa’s conversations in Casablanca.
keyFacts: The default style of Classical Hollywood
Keeps the spectator absorbed (passive)
Breaking it draws attention to the film’s construction
items.examTip: Contrast continuity with jump cuts for style questions.

items.definition: Meaning is created by joining shots; Kuleshov showed the same face reads differently after different images.
items.examples: City of God’s “Story of the Apartment”; Casablanca’s opening map montage.
keyFacts: Soviet montage (Eisenstein) creates ideas through collision of shots
A montage sequence compresses time
Spec names the Kuleshov effect directly
items.examTip: Montage is ideal for showing time and cycles.

items.term: Stylised editing: jump cuts, freeze-frames, split-screen
items.definition: Visible editing techniques that break continuity to create energy, shock or comment.
items.examples: Freeze-frames in City of God and Trainspotting; jump cuts in Bonnie and Clyde.
keyFacts: Jump cuts were popularised by the French New Wave
Freeze-frames fix a moment and a character
Split-screen shows simultaneous action
items.examTip: Connect stylised editing to an auteur signature.

items.definition: Shot length sets pace; cross-cutting between places builds tension or links ideas.
items.examples: Joker cross-cuts the TV studio with the riots; Get Out intercuts the silent auction.
keyFacts: Fast cutting = energy or panic; long takes = tension or realism
Cross-cutting implies a connection between two actions
Editing motifs repeat patterns of cutting
items.examTip: Describe the rhythm, not just “fast editing”.

items.definition: Effects created in post-production designed to engage the spectator and produce emotion.
items.examples: Pan’s Labyrinth mixes practical creatures with digital touch-ups.
keyFacts: Spec: the tension between intended and actual spectator response to VFX
Practical effects can feel more tactile than CGI
Digital grading and compositing are now standard
items.examTip: Links to the digital debate in Component 2.

items.definition: Diegetic sound exists in the story world; non-diegetic sound (score, narration) is heard only by the audience.
items.examples: Sam playing “As Time Goes By” (diegetic) becomes Steiner’s score (non-diegetic).
keyFacts: Sounds can move between the two
Voiceover is usually non-diegetic narration
Jukebox music in Shaun is diegetic
items.examTip: Always classify the sound before analysing it.

items.definition: Parallel sound matches the mood of the image; contrapuntal sound contrasts with it.
items.examples: “Perfect Day” over Renton’s overdose; bluegrass banjo over dangerous getaways.
keyFacts: Contrapuntal sound creates irony or unease
Parallel sound intensifies emotion
The distinction is named in the spec
items.examTip: A precise term that examiners reward.

items.definition: Layered effects, Foley, ambient sound, silence and repeated sound motifs build atmosphere and meaning.
items.examples: The spoon on the teacup in Get Out; Arthur’s laugh; the sweetened crunch of the bottle murder.
keyFacts: Multitrack mixing, asynchronous sound, Foley
Silence can be the most powerful sound
Sound motifs link characters and ideas
items.examTip: Pick one sound motif per film and learn its scenes.

items.definition: An original score or existing songs (needle-drops) shape emotion, period and meaning.
items.examples: Guðnadóttir’s cello (Joker); “Lust for Life” (Trainspotting); “Don’t Stop Me Now” (Shaun).
keyFacts: Leitmotif: a theme tied to a character or idea
Songs can comment ironically on the action
Music is a key cue for spectator response
items.examTip: Name the piece and its function.

items.definition: Classical star performance, Method acting, naturalism and improvisation create different effects.
items.examples: Bogart’s star persona; Phoenix’s Method-style transformation; City of God’s non-professional cast.
keyFacts: Method: the actor draws on inner experience
Improvisation brings spontaneity
Non-professional actors add authenticity
items.examTip: Compare performance styles across eras or films.

items.definition: Gesture, posture, facial expression and voice carry meaning beyond dialogue.
items.examples: Chris’s single tear; Vidal’s precise, preening movements; Arthur’s laugh.
keyFacts: The body can tell a story the dialogue hides
Vocal delivery: pace, pitch, accent
Interaction between actors creates relationships
items.examTip: Describe a specific gesture to earn the mark.

items.definition: Casting choices carry meaning through a star’s image or a non-actor’s authenticity.
items.examples: De Niro in Joker recalls Scorsese; Bogart’s tough-guy image shapes Rick.
keyFacts: Star theory (Dyer): stars are constructed images
Casting against type can surprise spectators
Casting is part of performance in the spec
items.examTip: Casting is a cue to spectator response.

items.definition: How films construct identities (gender, ethnicity, class, age) and places, including the ideology behind them.
items.examples: Liberal racism in Get Out; the favela in City of God; patriarchy in Pan’s Labyrinth.
keyFacts: Representations are constructed, never neutral
From 2029 the spec focuses on identity and place
Stereotypes can be reinforced or challenged
items.examTip: Always analyse representation through film form.

items.definition: How location and setting construct meaning, from a whole nation to a single neighbourhood.
items.examples: 1944 rural Spain; Rio’s favela; Renton’s Edinburgh; Shaun’s suburban London; Gotham as 1980s New York.
keyFacts: Place shaped by history, politics and national identity
Real locations vs studio sets
Place can be a character in itself
items.examTip: A strong angle for Global film questions.

items.definition: The overall look, sound and feel of a film and the pleasure or effect its style creates.
items.examples: Pan’s Labyrinth’s gothic fairytale; City of God’s kinetic, sun-drenched style.
keyFacts: Created by mise-en-scène, cinematography, lighting, music and editing together
The spec mentions the conflict between spectacle and narrative resolution
Aesthetics connect to auteur and ideology
items.examTip: Define the film’s aesthetic in one phrase before analysing it.

items.definition: Moments of visual spectacle can pause or compete with the drive towards narrative resolution.
items.examples: The Pale Man sequence; Arthur’s stair dance; Renton’s underwater swim.
keyFacts: Spectacle gives pleasure in itself
It can deepen meaning or distract from it
A good evaluative point in aesthetics answers
items.examTip: Use to show critical engagement with aesthetics.

topics.title: Core area 3: the contexts of film

items.definition: Social debates around the film’s production, such as those about ethnicity, gender or class.
items.examples: Post-Obama racial politics for Get Out; Gen-X slacker culture for Shaun.
keyFacts: Can be current (when made) or historical (when set)
Link to representation
Avoid generalised history lessons
items.examTip: One sentence of context, then straight into the film.

items.definition: Artistic movements, genres and cultural trends that shaped the film.
items.examples: The French New Wave for Bonnie and Clyde; Cinema Novo for City of God; Britpop for Trainspotting.
keyFacts: Spec example: “a significant film or artistic movement”
Intertextuality is a cultural link
Popular culture (music, fashion) also counts
items.examTip: Name the movement precisely.

items.definition: Political factors such as restrictions on free expression or movements for change.
items.examples: Francoism for Pan’s Labyrinth; Thatcherism for Trainspotting; WWII intervention for Casablanca.
keyFacts: Censorship (the Production Code) is political and institutional
Films can protest or support governments
Political context often drives ideology
items.examTip: Political context is the bridge to ideology questions.

items.definition: Who made and funded the film, how, and with what money, technology and constraints.
items.examples: Warner Bros. studio system; Blumhouse micro-budget; Channel 4 Films; Spanish–Mexican co-production.
keyFacts: Finance, distribution, technology, stars and censorship
Production constraints can create creative solutions
Explicit focus in Hollywood comparative study questions
items.examTip: Always include at least one number (budget, gross) per film.

items.definition: AO1: knowledge and understanding of film. AO2: applying it to analyse, compare and evaluate. Equal weight.
items.examples: A 40-mark answer is marked 20 for AO1 and 20 for AO2 across five bands.
keyFacts: AO1 rewards accurate terminology and knowledge
AO2 rewards analysis, comparison (Section A) and evaluation of critical approaches
If only one film is discussed in a two-film question, the mark is halved
items.examTip: Every paragraph needs both: knowledge (AO1) used to argue (AO2).

items.definition: Underline the command (how far / how useful), the focus and the instruction before planning.
items.examples: “How far... Refer in detail to at least one sequence from each film.”
keyFacts: How far / how useful / to what extent = make and argue a judgement
The focus is the lens (spectatorship, ideology, auteur, context)
The instruction tells you what evidence is required
items.examTip: Your biggest fix: answer THAT question, not everything you know.

items.definition: Point that answers the question, specific scene, named technique, meaning linked to the lens and the judgement.
items.examples: “To a significant extent... In the subway murders, low-key lighting and claustrophobic framing... aligning the spectator...”
keyFacts: Film form in EVERY paragraph (your teacher’s target 1)
Link back to the command words every time
Weave the second film in with “whereas” or “similarly”
items.examTip: Run every paragraph through the checklist on the Exam Kit page.

items.definition: Write impersonally: “the spectator is positioned”, never “I felt”.
items.examples: Replace “I think Joker makes me sympathise” with “Joker positions the spectator to sympathise”.
keyFacts: Your teacher’s target 3: no first person
“The spectator” lets you discuss different responses
Hedge with “arguably” and “to an extent”
items.examTip: Quick proofread for “I” before the end of the exam.

items.definition: Both papers are 2 hours 30 minutes; Component 1 has three 40-mark essays, so about 50 minutes each.
items.examples: Component 2: Global (40) about 60 minutes; Documentary, Silent and Experimental (20 each) about 30 minutes each.
keyFacts: Spend 5 minutes planning each essay
One question from a choice of two in each section
Leave 5 minutes to check judgement and conclusion
items.examTip: Plans: thesis + 3 to 4 scenes + judgement, in that order.
